strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: learning preferences from naturally occurring, multi-turn user feedback. The pipeline connects feedback detection, preference summarization, response generation, and preference training, producing a substantial dataset of 20,281 expert-response pairs.

Table 3 provides meaningful evidence of training utility across three model families and several established benchmarks. With GPT-4-generated data, AlpacaEval length-controlled win rates improve from 24.3% to 34.9% for Phi 3, 22.9% to 34.2% for LLaMA 3, and 17.1% to 31.4% for Mistral. These gains support a useful empirical contribution beyond the proposed evaluator.

The authors validate feedback detection using four human annotators on 50 conversations, report agreement and classification metrics, and explicitly separate evaluation users and conversations from training. The appendices provide detailed rubrics, annotation and evaluation prompts, model identifiers, and principal training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the contribution of in-situ feedback. Comparisons are primarily against models without additional training; there is no matched GPT-4 distillation baseline without feedback guidance, SFT-only ablation, or comparison with an existing preference dataset under comparable training budgets. Expert and on-policy variants also differ in dataset size, response provenance, and filtering. Consequently, the gains cannot be attributed specifically to authentic feedback rather than additional training or stronger teacher responses.

The central claim of improved alignment with actual users lacks independent validation. GPT-4 identifies feedback, summarizes preferences, generates expert responses, filters on-policy pairs, and judges the proposed evaluation. Figure 2 shows that supplying these summaries changes GPT-4's rankings, but does not establish greater agreement with users. Human validation covers SAT/DSAT detection only; it does not assess summary fidelity, generated pair correctness, or the modified evaluator. Correlation previously reported for WildBench does not establish validity for this adaptation.

The evidence for representative user preferences is limited. Only approximately 12.8% of conversations contain detected feedback, and DSAT recall is 48.4% despite 83.3% precision (Table 6). The evaluation additionally selects preferences most similar to others within task clusters and deliberately favors tasks resembling training data. This supports conclusions about selected, typical interactions, while leaving population coverage and minority preferences unresolved. The acknowledged selection bias substantially qualifies claims about diverse or 'true' human values.

The interpretation of results overstates their consistency. Section 5 claims that neither dataset variant compromises benchmark performance, yet on-policy Mistral declines on AlpacaEval LC (17.1% to 12.9%), Arena-Hard (12.6% to 10.3%), and MT-Bench (6.71 to 6.42). No uncertainty estimates or repeated-run results accompany claims of significant improvement, which particularly affects small changes such as GPT-4-trained Mistral's MT-Bench increase from 6.71 to 6.79.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful appendix details. The manuscript only promises a future dataset release and provides no implementation or split artifacts. Important construction details—including clustering embeddings, precise deduplication and filtering rules, and generation settings—are unspecified. It should also state explicitly whether preference system prompts are retained during training or supplied during evaluation generation. Together with the missing controlled comparisons and independent validation, these gaps warrant substantive revision before a Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: learning preferences from naturally occurring user feedback. The pipeline combines feedback detection, preference summarization, response generation, and preference training into a potentially useful resource containing 20,281 examples.

The GPT-4-generated dataset produces improvements across three model families and three external benchmarks. For example, Phi 3 improves from 24.3% to 34.9% on AlpacaEval’s length-controlled win rate and from 15.4% to 32.4% on Arena-Hard. These results support practical utility beyond the proposed evaluation metric.

The paper provides prompts, model identifiers, and core training hyperparameters, and explicitly separates training and test users and conversations. Its four-annotator audit of 50 conversations provides initial evidence for feedback-label quality, with model–human agreement approaching human–human agreement. Selection bias and harmful preferences are also acknowledged.
weaknesses: The central claim of closer alignment with actual users lacks independent validation. GPT-4o summarizes preferences, generates expert targets, and judges the custom evaluation. Figure 2 shows that providing the generation checklist to the evaluator changes its preferences; this does not establish improved agreement with users. The human study validates SAT/DSAT detection only, not preference-summary fidelity, generated response pairs, or final model rankings. A blinded human evaluation grounded in the original feedback is needed to substantiate these claims.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of user feedback. Comparisons are limited to the original instruction models and two WildFeedback variants. There is no matched GPT-4 response-generation baseline without extracted feedback, SFT-only ablation, or comparison against training on an existing preference dataset. Moreover, the GPT-4 dataset contains approximately twice as many examples as the on-policy datasets. Consequently, gains cannot be attributed specifically to feedback rather than teacher capability, additional training, or data quantity, and superiority over existing preference resources remains unsupported.

The custom test set provides limited evidence of population-level generalization. Section 4 deliberately selects central preferences within 70 clusters and favors tasks similar to training. This does not establish that the resulting 540 examples represent the majority of users. Coverage is further constrained by feedback being detected in only 12.8% of source conversations and DSAT recall of 48.4% in Table 6. The acknowledged selection bias should constrain the conclusions; claims about diverse human values and reduced bias require broader evaluation.

The claim that either dataset version preserves performance on other benchmarks directly contradicts Table 3. For Mistral, on-policy training reduces AlpacaEval LC from 17.1% to 12.9%, Arena-Hard from 12.6% to 10.3%, and MT-Bench from 6.71 to 6.42. Claims of significant improvements also lack confidence intervals or repeated-run evidence, which matters particularly for small changes such as Mistral’s GPT-4-data MT-Bench gain of 0.08.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix. The manuscript promises a future dataset release but supplies no dataset access or split identifiers. It also omits the embedding model and sufficient details of clustering, filtering, and the validation protocol used for hyperparameter selection. These omissions affect reconstruction of both the training resource and the custom benchmark. Together with the missing controls and independent validation, they warrant revision and resubmission next cycle rather than a positive Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: learning preferences from naturally occurring feedback in multi-turn conversations. The pipeline is practical, and the reported 20,281-pair dataset could be useful for conversational model training.

Table 3 provides substantive evidence that training on the GPT-4 version improves standard benchmark performance across three model families. For example, LLaMA 3’s AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate increases from 22.9% to 34.2%, and Phi 3’s Arena-Hard win rate increases from 15.4% to 32.4%. These results support the dataset’s practical utility.

The reported separation of training and evaluation users and conversations is a useful safeguard. The authors also conduct a human audit of feedback classification using four annotators and 50 conversations, rather than leaving this stage entirely unvalidated.

The high-level method is understandable, and the appendices provide classification and evaluation prompts, model identifiers, and major training hyperparameters. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges selection bias and potentially harmful feedback.
weaknesses: The central claim of improved alignment with actual users lacks independent validation. GPT-4 identifies feedback, summarizes preferences, generates expert responses, and judges alignment using those summaries. Figure 2 therefore demonstrates agreement with model-produced checklists, without establishing that the checklists faithfully capture users’ preferences or that checklist-guided judgments agree better with humans. The human audit validates only SAT/DSAT classification. Independent assessment grounded in the original feedback is needed for preference summaries, response rankings, and the proposed evaluation metric; claims about overcoming model biases and aligning with 'true human values' exceed the evidence.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of mined user feedback. Comparisons are primarily against untuned instruction models, without matched GPT-4 generation that omits feedback, SFT-only training, or training on an existing preference dataset. Consequently, the gains could substantially reflect additional training and stronger-teacher distillation. GPT-4 and on-policy datasets also differ in size and filtering, confounding their comparison. A matched feedback ablation is particularly important for substantiating the paper’s distinctive contribution.

The evidence for representative preference coverage is limited. DSAT recall is only 48.4%, with GPT–human kappa of 0.504, so the extraction pipeline misses substantial dissatisfaction even within the small audited sample. The 540-example evaluation further selects central preferences within clusters and explicitly favors tasks similar to training. This supports a narrower evaluation of common, familiar preferences; it does not establish coverage of the broader user population. Equal sampling from clusters also does not itself establish that the resulting preferences represent a population majority.

Some conclusions directly contradict the reported results. Section 5 states that neither dataset version compromises other benchmark performance, yet on-policy Mistral declines on AlpacaEval LC from 17.1% to 12.9%, Arena-Hard from 12.6% to 10.3%, and MT-Bench from 6.71 to 6.42. Its checklist-free evaluation also has more losses than wins. These tradeoffs require explicit discussion. Furthermore, no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variation across training runs support the repeated claims of significant improvements, particularly for small MT-Bench differences.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix. The manuscript promises a future dataset release but supplies no dataset or code link. Important construction details are unspecified, including the embedding model and exact clustering/selection procedure, response-generation decoding settings, treatment of SAT-only examples, and the validation criterion used for hyperparameter selection. strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: learning from feedback naturally expressed during user–LLM conversations. It presents a concrete pipeline producing 20,281 preference examples, with both GPT-4-generated and policy-generated response variants.

The GPT-4-data results provide meaningful evidence of practical utility across three model families. For example, Phi 3 improves from 24.3% to 34.9% on length-controlled AlpacaEval and from 15.4% to 32.4% on Arena-Hard. Length-controlled results help establish that the gains are not solely due to verbosity.

The feedback detector receives a human audit involving four annotators and 50 conversations. Its agreement with adjudicated labels approaches the reported human–human agreement, providing useful validation of this pipeline stage.

The manuscript supplies detailed annotation and evaluation prompts, model identifiers, and core training hyperparameters. The reported separation of test users and conversations from training is also a valuable safeguard.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the contribution of user feedback. Comparisons are against off-the-shelf models, without a matched control using GPT-4 responses generated on the same prompts without feedback, an SFT-only ablation, or training on an existing preference dataset. Consequently, improvements could substantially reflect teacher distillation and additional training. The expert/on-policy comparison also changes response sources, dataset sizes, and filtering, limiting causal interpretation.

The central claim of improved alignment with actual users lacks independent validation. GPT-4o summarizes preferences, generates expert responses, and judges responses against those summaries. Figure 2 demonstrates sensitivity to the supplied checklist, but does not establish that the checklist accurately represents users or that checklist-guided rankings agree better with human judgments. The human study evaluates SAT/DSAT classification only. A blinded audit of preference summaries and response rankings against the original feedback is needed.

The evaluation supports a narrower population claim than the manuscript makes. Section 4 deliberately selects preferences resembling others within task clusters and emphasizes similarity to training tasks. This does not establish representation of majority preferences or generalization across diverse users. Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied prompts and training settings. The dataset is only promised for future release, and the manuscript does not sufficiently specify generation settings, the preference-filtering procedure, clustering representations, or hyperparameter-selection criteria. These omissions affect reconstruction of both the training data and the custom benchmark. Together with the missing controls and independent preference validation, they warrant revision next cycle before a sound Findings recommendation.

Substantial improvements over the starting models support practical utility beyond the proposed evaluator: Phi-3's AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate increases from 24.3% to 34.9%, and Arena-Hard performance from 15.4% to 32.4%.

The paper reports conversation- and user-disjoint evaluation, human validation of feedback detection and checklist evaluation, detailed annotation rubrics, model identifiers, and core training hyperparameters. DSAT precision of 83.3% supports the feasibility of mining useful feedback. Selection bias and unsafe preferences are explicitly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The central claim of improved alignment with actual users is insufficiently validated. GPT-4 extracts preferences, generates preferred responses, filters on-policy pairs, and evaluates responses using those extracted preferences. Increased checklist scores therefore establish adherence to inferred preferences more directly than faithful recovery of users' preferences. The 200-conversation human study reports 57.14% agreement versus 63.27% human-human agreement, but evaluates checklist application rather than independently validating preference extraction or demonstrating improved user alignment in the trained models.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of conversational feedback. WildFeedback and regenerated UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversational context, and response-selection procedures. A control using the same WildChat prompts and comparable generation budgets without feedback, or with generic refinement instructions, is needed to distinguish feedback-specific benefits from domain matching and distillation. No SFT-only comparison establishes the additional benefit of the constructed preference pairs.

Reproducibility remains incomplete for a contribution centered on a dataset and custom benchmark. The dataset is described as 'available soon,' without an accompanying artifact link. The FAISS-based test construction omits the embedding model and sufficient similarity and deduplication details; the hyperparameter search does not specify its validation and selection protocol. These gaps materially limit reconstruction despite the useful prompts and final training settings.

The claims of consistent and significant superiority over UltraFeedback exceed the reported results. For Qwen-2 with GPT-4-generated data, WildFeedback scores below UltraFeedback on AlpacaEval LC (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66). Several other advantages are small, and no confidence intervals or training-seed variability are reported.

The evaluation supports a narrower population than the claims about diverse, evolving user needs and majority preferences suggest. Feedback-bearing conversations are selective, DSAT recall is only 48.4%, and the custom test deliberately selects central preferences within clusters and tasks resembling training data. The acknowledged selection bias is therefore consequential to interpreting the results. Together with the missing controls and incomplete reproducibility, this leaves the paper borderline for Findings despite credible benchmark gains.

Experiments cover three model families and three established benchmarks, providing evidence beyond the proposed evaluator. For example, Phi-3 trained on WF GPT-4 improves AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate from 24.3% to 34.9% and Arena-Hard from 15.4% to 32.4% (Table 3). Regenerating UltraFeedback responses is also a useful effort toward stronger comparisons.

The feedback detector receives substantive human validation: 50 conversations containing over 500 utterances are annotated, with disagreements adjudicated. DSAT precision reaches 83.3%, and model–human agreement approaches human–human agreement (Table 6), supporting the feasibility of mining useful feedback.

The pipeline is understandable, with model identifiers, extensive prompts, and principal SFT/DPO hyperparameters documented. The reported separation of training and test users and conversations is appropriate, and the limitations acknowledge selection bias and harmful preferences.

Experiments demonstrate practical utility across three model families and three established benchmarks. For example, Phi-3’s AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate improves from 24.3% to 34.9%, and its Arena-Hard win rate improves from 15.4% to 32.4%. Regenerating UltraFeedback responses with the same model families strengthens the comparison.

The paper includes meaningful human validation: feedback classification is checked on 50 conversations containing over 500 utterances, and checklist evaluation on 200 conversations. Reporting human–human agreement alongside model–human agreement provides useful calibration. Separating training and test conversations and users is also appropriate.

The dataset link, model identifiers, annotation and evaluation prompts, and principal SFT/DPO hyperparameters provide a reasonable basis for reproducing the core approach. Together with the benchmark improvements, this supports a Findings-level empirical and resource contribution.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the contribution of actual user feedback. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversation length, response construction, and filtering. A controlled comparison using identical WildChat prompts and generation procedures, with versus without extracted feedback, would establish whether feedback drives the gains. An SFT-only ablation would also clarify the added value of preference optimization.

The stronger claims about authentic user alignment and reduced model bias remain insufficiently validated. GPT-4 extracts preferences, generates responses, filters pairs, and judges outcomes, allowing correlated biases across stages. Table 9 reports 57.14% agreement and κ=0.372 against human judgments, but does not establish that checklist guidance improves agreement over unguided evaluation. The fidelity of the extracted preference summaries to the original feedback is not separately audited.

The custom benchmark supports a restricted generalization claim. Selecting central preferences within 70 clusters and emphasizing tasks similar to training does not establish that the resulting 540 examples represent majority preferences. Feedback detection also has only 48.4% DSAT recall, despite 83.3% precision. A randomly sampled user-disjoint evaluation and results by feedback type would better characterize coverage.

Several other differences are small, and confidence intervals or variation across training seeds are not reported.

Exact replication remains underdocumented despite the useful implementation appendix. Missing details include generation decoding settings, context truncation, clustering embeddings and deduplication rules, and the validation criterion used for hyperparameter selection. These omissions limit confidence in reproducing the precise comparisons.

strengths: WildFeedback addresses an important NLP problem: learning from feedback that users naturally provide during conversations. The 20,281-example dataset, accompanying preference summaries, and model-specific variants constitute a potentially useful resource beyond the proposed training pipeline.

The experiments provide credible evidence of training utility across three model families and three established benchmarks. For example, Phi-3 trained on WF GPT-4 improves from 24.3 to 34.9 on AlpacaEval’s length-controlled win rate and from 15.4 to 32.4 on Arena-Hard. These external benchmark results strengthen the evidence beyond the proposed checklist evaluation.

The paper includes meaningful validation and documentation: human annotation studies with human-human agreement baselines, regenerated UltraFeedback comparisons, reported separation of training and test users and conversations, detailed prompts, and major training hyperparameters. The pipeline is understandable, and the limitations acknowledge noisy feedback and selection bias.
weaknesses: The central claim of more faithful alignment with real users needs stronger independent validation. GPT-4 extracts preference summaries, generates or filters training pairs, and judges the resulting responses. Figure 2 establishes that checklists influence judgments, but does not establish that those judgments better recover users’ preferences. Appendix C reports 57.14% agreement with humans (κ=0.372), against 63.27% human-human agreement, without comparing checklist and checklist-free accuracy against independently verified preferences. Auditing summary faithfulness and pair labels against the original feedback would address the main concern preventing a clear Findings recommendation.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of authentic feedback. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt source, conversational context, response construction, and filtering. Consequently, their comparison cannot determine how much improvement comes from feedback conditioning versus other dataset differences. A controlled experiment on the same WildChat prompts using genuine feedback, omitted feedback, and generic revision instructions would substantially strengthen the methodological claim.

The 540-example evaluation set deliberately selects central preferences within clusters and tasks resembling training tasks. This supports evaluation on that curated population, but does not establish representativeness of the majority of users. Feedback selection and the detector’s 48.4% DSAT recall further restrict coverage. Claims about diverse, evolving user preferences and reduced bias exceed the demonstrated scope.

Claims of consistent, significant superiority over UltraFeedback are overstated. In Table 3, Qwen-2 WF GPT-4 underperforms UF GPT-4 on AlpacaEval LC (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66); several other improvements are small. Confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are absent, limiting confidence in the comparative advantages despite the clearer gains over the original models.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendices. The manuscript does not sufficiently specify the embeddings and clustering procedure, exact split and user-grouping construction, generation settings, or hyperparameter-selection protocol. It should also explicitly state whether extracted preference summaries are supplied to the trained models during training and inference, beyond their documented use in response synthesis and judging.

strengths: The strongest contribution is a useful NLP resource: 20,281 preference pairs constructed from naturally occurring conversational feedback, with additional model-specific variants. The dataset and demonstrated training benefits support a Findings recommendation.

Experiments cover three model families, expert-generated and on-policy data, and three established benchmarks alongside the proposed evaluation. Improvements extend beyond the custom metric: Phi-3’s AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate rises from 24.3% to 34.9%, and Arena-Hard performance rises from 15.4% to 32.4%. Regenerating UltraFeedback responses provides a more relevant baseline than using its original responses unchanged.

Human validation provides useful checks on both feedback identification and checklist judging. Reporting human–human agreement alongside model–human agreement makes annotation ambiguity visible. The 83.3% precision for dissatisfaction detection supports its use for mining training examples.

The pipeline is clearly organized, and the dataset link, annotation rubrics, prompts, model identifiers, training hyperparameters, and compute estimates provide substantial support for reuse. The reported separation of users and conversations between training and testing is also appropriate.
weaknesses: The experiments establish the usefulness of the complete recipe more clearly than the specific benefit of natural user feedback. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversation length, negative-response construction, filtering, and dataset size. A comparison using the same WildFeedback prompts with feedback omitted or replaced by generic guidance would better isolate the contribution. An SFT-only ablation would also distinguish response distillation from preference-training benefits.

The claim that checklist evaluation more accurately captures real user preferences remains insufficiently validated. GPT-4 extracts preferences, generates expert responses, filters on-policy pairs, and judges the custom benchmark, creating correlated sources of error. On 200 conversations, judge–human agreement is 57.14% with kappa 0.372, versus human–human agreement of 63.27% with kappa 0.436. This is useful but limited validation; there is no corresponding human-agreement comparison showing that checklists improve evaluation accuracy. Figure 2 demonstrates sensitivity to the supplied checklist, rather than independently establishing fidelity to users.

The 540-example test set deliberately selects preference-central examples within 70 clusters and favors tasks resembling training tasks. This evaluates a restricted distribution and does not establish that the selected examples represent the majority of users. Together with dissatisfaction detection recall of only 48.4%, this limits conclusions about coverage of diverse preferences. The broader claims about addressing subjectivity and model bias exceed the demonstrated evidence.

Claims of consistently and significantly outperforming UltraFeedback overstate Table 3. For example, Qwen-2 with WF GPT-4 scores below UF GPT-4 on AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66). Several other differences are small, and confidence intervals, repeated training runs, or significance analyses are not reported.

Exact reproduction would benefit from additional specification of the clustering embeddings and settings, user-grouping procedure, preference-generation decoding parameters, and validation criterion used for hyperparameter selection. Appendix A.2 documents preference extraction but does not provide the complete response-generation template. These gaps limit reproducibility of the construction and evaluation pipeline despite the otherwise helpful documentation.
